lead: A regular expression is a formula. A finite automaton is a machine. Kleene's theorem says these two, and every variant in between, describe exactly the same languages: anything you can write as a formula you can build as a machine, and anything a machine accepts you can write as a formula. The theorem gives you a choice of tool — describe a pattern the easy way, then convert. It is what lets grep compile a pattern into a state machine, a compiler turn token rules into a lexer, and a form validator reject bad input in one pass over the text.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for regular-expression syntax and Unit 1, Deterministic finite automata (DFA) and Nondeterministic finite automata (NFA), for the machines.

sections.h3: One theorem, four ways to say the same thing

blocks.text: A language L over an alphabet Σ is regular when some DFA accepts it. Separately, a regular expression over Σ denotes a language: ∅ denotes no strings, ε denotes the single empty string, each symbol a ∈ Σ denotes {a}, and union, concatenation and Kleene star build larger languages from smaller ones. The two definitions look unrelated. Kleene's theorem says they describe the same collection of languages.
L is regular ⇔ L = L(M) for some DFA M ⇔ L = L(M) for some NFA M ⇔ L = L(r) for some regular expression r
blocks.where: L(M) is the set of strings the machine M accepts; L(r) is the set of strings the expression r denotes. The four statements are about one and the same language L, over one finite alphabet Σ.

blocks.text: The first equivalence is the definition. The second was proved in Unit 1, NFA and DFA equivalence by subset construction: every NFA can be turned into a DFA with the same language. The new content is the last one, proved in two halves — every regular expression becomes an ε-NFA accepting the same language, and every DFA becomes a regular expression denoting the same language. Some syllabi call this the equivalence of finite automata and regular expressions; others call it Kleene's theorem.

The intuition is finiteness. A regular expression is a finite formula; an automaton has finitely many states. Both remember a bounded amount about the input read so far, and neither can count without a limit. That shared limitation is why the two notations match exactly, and why they fail on exactly the same languages.

sections.h3: The round trip: how each half is proved

blocks.text: The proof is a loop with three edges. Each edge is an algorithm, and each leaves the accepted language unchanged.

items: Regex → ε-NFA, Thompson's construction. Build two-state machines for ∅, ε and each symbol; join machines for subexpressions with fresh states and ε-transitions for union, concatenation and star. Let m be the number of symbols and operators in the expression (for a*, m = 2). The construction gives at most 2m states. See Chapter 2.3.

ε-NFA → DFA, subset construction. Each new state is a set of old states, closed under ε-transitions; a set is final if it holds a final state. An n-state NFA gives at most 2ⁿ DFA states. See Unit 1, NFA and DFA equivalence.
DFA → regex, Arden's theorem or state elimination. Write one equation per state, then solve for the start state, eliminating states one at a time. See Chapter 2.4.

blocks.text: Edges 1 and 2 take a regular expression to a DFA, giving the direction regular expression → DFA. Edge 3 takes a DFA to a regular expression, giving DFA → regular expression. With the Unit 1 equivalence between NFA and DFA, all four statements stand or fall together.

Two cautions. The 2m and 2ⁿ figures are upper bounds, not promises of small machines: a small DFA can need a long regular expression. And the loop passes through an ε-NFA, so a missed ε-closure in the middle edge quietly changes the language, and the argument collapses.

items: Closure under union, concatenation and star comes free: these are the three regular-expression operators, and each has an automaton construction that keeps the language regular.

Closure under intersection (and union) comes from the product construction on two DFAs. Closure under complement comes from taking a complete DFA, making final states non-final and non-final states final; this is why the DFA must be deterministic and complete. See Chapter 2.7.
Membership: run the DFA on the string w. Time is O(|w|), whatever notation you started from.
Emptiness: check whether any final state is reachable from the start state.
Equivalence of two descriptions: convert both to DFAs, minimise both with the table-filling algorithm from Unit 1, and compare the results.

blocks.text: The practical gain is freedom of description. A pattern that is easy to write as a formula, such as [a-z]+@[a-z]+\.(com|in), can be compiled to a machine and run in linear time. A machine that is easy to draw, such as the parity machine in the example below, can be turned into a formula when you want an algebraic proof.

What the theorem does not give you is a test for non-regularity. It only says that if a language has an automaton it has a formula, and the reverse. To show a language has neither, you need the pumping lemma.

figure.caption: Each arrow is an algorithm that keeps the language unchanged, so all three boxes describe the same languages; follow the loop in either direction to convert.

spec.title: Kleene's theorem: one loop, three conversions
spec.aria: A cycle of three equivalent views — regular expression to epsilon-NFA by Thompson's construction, epsilon-NFA to DFA by subset construction, and DFA back to regular expression by Arden's theorem or state elimination.

examples.question: Let L = {w ∈ {0,1}* : w contains an even number of 1s}. (a) Give a DFA for L and list its transitions. (b) Give a regular expression for L. (c) Say why L is regular, quoting Kleene's theorem. (d) How many strings of length at most 3 does L contain?
steps: Parity is all that matters, so two states suffice. q0 means 'an even number of 1s read so far', q1 means 'odd'. Start in q0, because the empty string has zero 1s, and make q0 final.
A 0 never changes the count: δ(q0,0) = q0 and δ(q1,0) = q1. A 1 always flips parity: δ(q0,1) = q1 and δ(q1,1) = q0. This DFA has two states.
Regular expression: 0* covers any run of 0s. Each block 10*10* contains exactly two 1s, so (10*10*)* keeps the count even. The full expression is 0*(10*10*)*.
Part (c): a DFA accepts L, so L is regular by definition; Kleene's theorem then guarantees a regular expression exists, and the expression in step 3 is that witness.
Part (d): count by length. Length 0: ε, accepted, 1 string. Length 1: 0, accepted, 1 string. Length 2: 00 and 11, 2 strings. Length 3: 000, 011, 101, 110, 4 strings. Total 1 + 1 + 2 + 4 = 8 strings.
examples.answer: L is regular: a two-state parity DFA and the regular expression 0*(10*10*)* both describe it, and L contains 8 strings of length at most 3.

traps: The theorem does not say every language is regular. It says the automaton world and the formula world are the same size. {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0} has no DFA and no regular expression, and both fail together.
∅ and ε are different regular expressions. ∅ denotes no strings at all; ε denotes exactly one string, the empty one. Writing ε where you mean ∅ changes the language while looking harmless.
In the middle edge of the loop, forgetting ε-closures in the subset construction produces a DFA for a different language. The theorem stays true; your conversion is what is wrong.

The bounds are upper bounds: an expression with m symbols and operators gives an ε-NFA with at most 2m states (for a*, m = 2, so 4 states), and an n-state NFA gives a DFA with at most 2ⁿ states. A short formula can need a huge machine.

A question asking 'prove L is regular' wants a DFA, an NFA or a regular expression. An English description of L earns nothing until you build one of the three or quote closure properties from Chapter 2.7.

quiz.q: State Kleene's theorem for a language L over an alphabet Σ.
quiz.a: L is regular if and only if some DFA accepts L, if and only if some NFA (or ε-NFA) accepts L, if and only if some regular expression denotes L.

quiz.q: Why does the proof need the ε-NFA → DFA step, when Thompson's construction already produces a machine?
quiz.a: Thompson produces an ε-NFA, and the conversions described in this book (Arden's theorem, state elimination) are worked on DFAs here, so the subset construction bridges to them and closes the loop. State elimination can in fact be applied to an ε-NFA directly, giving the same result.

quiz.q: Kleene's theorem is often read as 'regular expressions and finite automata are equally powerful'. Explain what 'equally powerful' means here, and give one language that both fail on.
quiz.a: Both describe exactly the class of regular languages: every expression has an equivalent automaton and every automaton has an equivalent expression, so neither can describe more than the other. Both fail on {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0}, which needs unbounded counting.

quiz.q: Over Σ = {0,1}, give a regular expression and a DFA for the language of strings ending in 01.
quiz.a: Expression: (0+1)*01. States: q0 start (nothing useful seen), q1 (last symbol was 0), q2 final (last two symbols are 01). Transitions: δ(q0,0)=q1, δ(q0,1)=q0, δ(q1,0)=q1, δ(q1,1)=q2, δ(q2,0)=q1, δ(q2,1)=q0.

quiz.q: The worked example's DFA has two states q0 (even, start, final) and q1 (odd). Write its state equations for the Arden conversion and state the solution.
quiz.a: X0 = ε + X0·0 + X1·1 and X1 = X0·1 + X1·0. Arden's rule on X1 gives X1 = X0·10*, so X0 = ε + X0(0 + 10*1) and X0 = (0 + 10*1)*. That denotes the same language as 0*(10*10*)*.

quiz.q: L is a regular language and M is not regular. What can you conclude about L ∪ M, L ∩ M and L·M? Justify each.
quiz.a: No definite conclusion for any of the three. For union and intersection: if L = Σ*, then L ∪ M = Σ* (regular) while L ∩ M = M (not regular); if L = ∅, then L ∪ M = M (not regular) while L ∩ M = ∅ (regular). For concatenation: if L = Σ*, then L·M = Σ* (regular); if L = {ε}, which is regular, then L·M = M (not regular). The result therefore depends on L, so no closure property decides it in one step.

beyond: Not for the exam. This equivalence proof is why grep and compiler lexers are fast: the pattern is compiled into an automaton and the input is scanned once. Real engines split two ways — RE2 and the Rust regex crate simulate the automaton and never backtrack, while PCRE-style engines backtrack and can be very slow on some patterns. Backreferences such as (a+)\1 step outside the regular languages altogether, so those engines do more than Kleene's theorem allows. Libraries also build automata straight from formulas using Brzozowski derivatives. Search next: Thompson NFA simulation, Brzozowski derivative, DFA minimisation in lexers.
